chunks: "The big advantage is that an N-channel FET is simply a better switch.
Electrons are two to three times more mobile than holes, so for the same die size an NFET has two to three times lower on-resistance and less gate charge.
That means less conduction loss, faster switching, smaller and cheaper parts, and many more to choose from.
At 10 amps, a 10 milliohm NFET dissipates 1 watt where a comparable-cost PFET at 25 milliohm dissipates 2. 5. The challenge is the gate drive.
An NFET turns on when its gate is a few volts above its source . On the high side the source is the switch node, and when the FET is on that node is at the supply.
So to turn on a high-side NFET in a 24 volt bridge the gate has to go to about 34 volts, higher than anything I have in the system.
I need a floating gate supply that follows the switch node: usually a bootstrap capacitor charged through a diode while the low side is on, or a charge pump.

Bootstrap needs the low side to turn on periodically, which limits maximum duty cycle, and it can't hold the FET on forever because the capacitor droops, so motor drivers add a charge pump for 100% duty.
Start-up is trickier because the capacitor starts empty. The switch node undershoots below ground and has fast dv/dt that can upset the level shifter.
So it's more parts and more layout care, in exchange for efficiency."
